passages.title: Task 1
passages.text:
(1) Many of the objects we use every day were not planned at all. They began as mistakes, or as experiments that went in an unexpected direction. What turned these accidents into inventions was not luck alone, but the curiosity of the people who noticed them.

(2) Take the microwave oven. In the 1940s, an American engineer named Percy Spencer was working with radar equipment when he noticed that a chocolate bar in his pocket had melted. Instead of simply cleaning his pocket, he wondered why it had happened. He soon tried heating other foods, and within a few years the first microwave ovens were on sale.

(3) Sticky notes have a similar story. In 1968, a scientist at an American company was trying to make a very strong glue but produced a weak one instead. It could stick to paper and be removed without leaving a mark, yet for years nobody knew what to do with it. Then a colleague who sang in a church choir needed bookmarks that would not fall out of his song book, and he remembered the weak glue.

(4) Historians of science say these stories share an important pattern. In each case, the inventor recognised the value of something that other people would have thrown away. "Chance favours the prepared mind," said the French scientist Louis Pasteur in the nineteenth century, and the history of invention seems to prove him right.

(5) For students, the lesson is encouraging. Mistakes are not always failures. A failed experiment can become a starting point, but only for someone who stops, asks why, and is willing to try again.
